title: BitFuFu Announces June 2026 Bitcoin Production and Operational Updates
summary: BitFuFu released its unaudited June 2026 operational report, posting 125 BTC in monthly production and 1,671 BTC in holdings....
body_text: SINGAPORE, July 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- BitFuFu Inc. (“BitFuFu” or the “Company”) (NASDAQ: FUFU), a world-leading Bitcoin miner and mining services innovator, today announced its unaudited Bitcoin production and operational metrics for June 2026. “During June, we continued executing our long-term strategy with a focus on enhancing operational quality and capital discipline,” said Leo Lu, Chairman and CEO of BitFuFu. “While optimizing our mining operations, we acquired and deployed 1,200 S21 XP units in June, increasing our self-owned hashrate to 3.5 EH/s. We have also signed agreements to acquire and deploy 2,000 additional S21 XP units in July, with full operational deployment expected to be completed during the month. In addition, during June, we secured 5.3 EH/s of hashrate from suppliers under a nine-month agreement, scheduled to commence in August 2026, reflecting our conviction in Bitcoin's medium- to long-term value proposition. Together with our recently announced share repurchase program, we remain focused on disciplined capital allocation, optimizing asset utilization, and investing in the infrastructure and technologies that support our long-term growth and create sustainable value for shareholders.” June 2026 Highlights (as of June 30, 2026) June 2026 May 2026 Bitcoin Held 1,671 BTC 1,855 BTC Bitcoin Production 125 BTC 177 BTC Daily Bitcoin Production 4.2 BTC 5.7 BTC Self-Mining Production 70 BTC 90 BTC Cloud Mining Production 55 BTC 87 BTC Hashrate 15.3 EH/s 19.5 EH/s Self-Owned Hashrate 3.5 EH/s 3.2 EH/s Hashrate from Third-Party Suppliers and Hosting Customers 11.8 EH/s 16.3 EH/s Average Fleet Efficiency 17.9 J/TH 17.8 J/TH Power Capacity 273 MW 346 MW Bitcoin Holdings and Production: Bitcoin Held: 1,671 BTC1. The reduction in Bitcoin holdings during June mainly reflects the net impact of client receipts and upfront payments to suppliers for 5.3EH/s of future hashrate capacity, scheduled to commence in August 2026 and extend for 270 days. Bitcoin Production: 125 BTC (including 55 BTC from cloud mining and 70 BTC from self-mining), representing a 29.4% month-over-month decrease, which was primarily due to the decrease in the total hashrate under management. Daily bitcoin production averaged 4.2 BTC throughout June, with contributions from both cloud mining and self-mining operations. Hashrate Overview: Total Hashrate Under Management: 15.3 EH/s, compared with 19.5 EH/s in May 2026. Self-Owned Hashrate 2 : 3.5 EH/s, representing a 9.4% month-over-month increase, reflecting continued growth in the company's self-operated mining capacity. Hashrate from Third-Party Suppliers and Hosting Customers2: 11.8 EH/s. Average Fleet Efficiency: 17.9 J/TH, demonstrating consistently efficient mining operations. Power and Infrastructure: Total Power Capacity Under Management: 273 MW. About BitFuFu Inc. BitFuFu Inc. is a world-leading Bitcoin miner and mining services innovator. BitFuFu is committed to empowering the global Bitcoin network through its industry-leading cloud mining platform, rapidly scaling infrastructure, and innovative mining services. For more information, visit ir.bitfufu.com or follow BitFuFu on X @ BitFuFuOfficial . title: How an Automatic License Plate Recognition System Works
summary: Learn how an automatic license plate recognition system helps law enforcement or business security teams look for vehicle information after a safety incident occurs.
body_text: What an Automatic License Plate Recognition System Does An automatic license plate recognition system helps law enforcement or business security teams look for vehicle information after a safety incident occurs. License plate reader cameras capture an image of a vehicle, then software turns the plate and supported vehicle details into searchable information. For city councils, municipal leaders, neighborhood associations, and residents, the most important question is not whether the camera can read a plate. The important question is whether the automatic license plate recognition program has a clear purpose and complies with local laws around access, data retention, and sharing before cameras go live. How ALPR Turns Vehicle Images Into Investigatory Leads An automatic license plate recognition system works in a simple sequence: a camera sees a vehicle, the system reads the plate and supported vehicle details, then the record is saved with time and location. A typical ALPR deployment process looks like this: Cameras are placed in locations such as roadways, parking lot entrances, or shared access points. The camera captures a vehicle image as the vehicle passes through the camera’s field of view. Software reads the plate and supported vehicle details, which may include make, color, body type, and distinguishing characteristics when available. The system adds time and location, so the detection can be searched, mapped, reviewed, or connected to a reported incident. Customer-configured hot lists can generate alerts for vehicles of interest, such as stolen vehicles, AMBER Alerts, active warrants, or locally defined case needs. The system does not decide whether enforcement action should occur. An ALPR alert is a lead or a piece of evidence that requires human review, corroboration, and use under applicable law and local policy. What ALPR Captures and What IT Does Not Capture ALPR systems capture vehicle-related information. A typical read can include plate text, supported state information, vehicle images, time, location, and supported vehicle attributes such as make, color, body type, and distinguishing characteristics when the system can identify them. Those details matter because incidents often start with incomplete information. A person may remember a dark SUV, a partial plate, a certain direction of travel, or a rough time window. ALPR can help authorized reviewers compare those details against vehicle detections and decide what deserves additional review. ALPR data is not the same as a personal identity record. It is not tied to names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, or addresses. Flock’s ALPR has no facial recognition technology, and Flock ALPR cameras are not used for monitoring speed or issuing traffic citations. Flock does not sell customer data, and customers control whether and how their data is shared. Flock addresses common ALPR concerns directly in " Does Flock Enable Mass Surveillance? " and the license plate reader myths guide . How ALPR Can Support City and Public Safety Work ALPR is most useful when it is tied to a defined safety need. Cities and communities may use ALPR to alert public safety teams to vehicles of interest, or support review after a reported incident. Common uses include: Logging vehicle activity at roadways, parking lot entrances, neighborhood access points, business corridors, and other priority locations. Sending real-time alerts when a vehicle on a customer-configured hot list is detected by LPR cameras. Searching detections after an incident using a plate, partial plate, vehicle description, time window, or location. Adding case notes, reports, or photos to custom hot list alerts when policy allows, so reviewers understand why an alert matters. Coordinating across agencies, neighborhoods, businesses, and law enforcement partners under defined data-sharing rules. For a city manager, ALPR can reduce the time teams spend reviewing disconnected footage. For a neighborhood association, ALPR can provide vehicle evidence after an incident without asking residents to confront people directly. For local businesses, ALPR can help connect activity outside a property to a reported theft, break-in, or safety concern. The purpose is better vehicle evidence and faster review. How Communities Should Govern ALPR Data Responsible ALPR deployment starts before the first camera is installed. Public officials and community stakeholders should be able to explain why the system is being used, who can access the data, how long detections are kept, when sharing is allowed, and how misuse is detected and addressed. A practical governance review should answer: Who may access ALPR system data, alerts, and searches What training is required before access is granted What context is required for each query How long vehicle data is retained How access, searches, alerts, and sharing are audited When data may be shared with another agency or partner, and who approves it How law enforcement access works when a private or community customer owns the data How alert matches and possible false positives are reviewed before follow-up How residents are informed about purpose, placement, retention, oversight, and limits How the program aligns with state law, local ordinance, agency policy, and community expectations Flock data is automatically deleted after 30 days by default, unless a different retention period is required by the customer. Customers own their data, and Flock does not share it without authorization. Searches require documented reasons, and use of the system can be reviewed through audit trails. State and local rules may add additional requirements. Flock’s explanation of SB40 and ALPR use in New Mexico shows how one statewide framework addresses ALPR collection, sharing, retention, access, and prohibited uses. What Deployment Involves Deploying an automatic license plate recognition system is a planning exercise, not just a camera purchase. The right plan starts with the safety question the community is trying to answer, then places cameras only where vehicle detections can support that purpose. A deployment plan should cover: Coverage planning, including where cameras should be placed and where they should not be placed Power and connectivity options Integration with existing safety or security processes, including alert review and evidence sharing Implementation and maintenance expectations, including installation, support, and system health User training and administrator responsibilities Public communication, including how residents or stakeholders will understand what the system does and what limits apply What to Evaluate Before Choosing an ALPR System Choosing an ALPR system should come down to whether the system is accurate and compliant with local policy. Plate reads matter, but a system also needs to help people review results carefully and explain how the program is governed. Evaluation criteria should include: Vehicle identification beyond plate text, including supported attributes such as make, color, body type, and distinguishing traits Performance when plates are temporary, partial, obscured, missing, covered, or swapped Day and night reliability, including low-light and no-light image performance Search and alert usability for people who need to work quickly Integrations with existing tools Installation expectations, maintenance, support, and system health monitoring Training, permissions, auditability, retention settings, and sharing limits Public-facing resources that help residents understand purpose, policy, and safeguards How Flock Supports Responsible ALPR Usage The Flock platform connects ALPR data with investigation, response, and governance tools so teams can work from clearer evidence and documented controls. Capabilities include: LPR detections that convert vehicle images into searchable data for investigative and security use. Real-time alerts when customer-configured hot lists detect vehicles of interest. Vehicle identification using supported attributes beyond plate text, including make, color, body type, and distinguishing traits where available. Search tools that can support partial information, vehicle descriptions, and reviewable case context. Governance controls that support permissions, retention settings, audit trails, sharing rules, and policy-aligned use. Flock gives customers the tools to run ALPR programs with clearer context and stronger accountability. Customers remain responsible for using the technology according to applicable laws, policies, and their own oversight requirements. To evaluate an ALPR deployment for a city, neighborhood, business, or community setting, talk with Flock or explore the broader Flock public safety platform . FAQs What Does an Automatic License Plate Recognition System Not Capture? An automatic license plate recognition system captures vehicle-related data, including plate text, time, location, and vehicle attributes such as make, color, body type, and distinguishing characteristics when available. The Flock license plate reader cameras overview explains how vehicle data becomes searchable vehicle evidence. Flock's automatic license plate recognition system does not identify drivers or passengers, use facial recognition, record conversations, track phones, determine immigration status, or make enforcement decisions on its own. Flock's ALPR data is not tied to names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, or addresses. How Accurate Are ALPR Systems, and What Affects False Positives? ALPR accuracy depends on whether the camera can get a clear vehicle image. Plate visibility, lighting, camera placement, vehicle speed, weather, plate condition, and the review process can all affect results. Flock’s LPR achieves over 98% plate capture, over 96% OCR accuracy, and over 97% plate-state accuracy. An ALPR read should be treated as an investigative lead that requires human review and corroboration, not as a standalone basis for enforcement action. Flock addresses related misconceptions in its license plate reader myths guide . What Does ALPR Deployment Involve for a city, community, neighborhood, or business? ALPR deployment involves deciding where cameras belong, how they will be powered and connected, who can use the system, how alerts will be reviewed, how data will be retained, and how the public will understand the program. Cost depends on coverage needs, camera quantity, placement, deployment model, software capabilities, integrations, maintenance, and support. How Should Communities Govern ALPR Data Access, Retention, and Sharing? Communities should set clear rules for who can access ALPR detections, what search reasons are required, how long data is retained, how use is audited, when sharing is allowed, and how residents are informed. Flock data is automatically deleted after 30 days by default unless a different retention period is required by the customer. Customers own their data and control sharing. Flock’s discussion of SB40 and ALPR use in New Mexico shows how formal policy can define those responsibilities.

title: PGE secures more than 1,000 MW of new clean energy and battery storage, advances additional projects to support reliable, affordable service
summary: Portland General Electric has finalized agreements for more than 1,000 megawatts of new clean energy and battery storage, marking major progress in the company’s largest clean energy acquisition effort to date.
body_text: PORTLAND, Ore. — Portland General Electric has finalized agreements for more than 1,000 megawatts of new clean energy and battery storage, marking major progress in the company’s largest clean energy acquisition effort to date. The investments — along with the advancement of the next round of clean energy projects — are part of a long-term strategy to keep power safe, affordable, reliable and increasingly clean for Oregon customers. As part of its Integrated Resource Planning process, PGE plans years ahead to make sure customers have the energy they need. This includes securing new renewable resources, adding battery storage to support reliability, strengthening the grid, and capturing federal tax incentives that help reduce customer costs. A multi-pronged process to identify the least-cost, least-risk projects PGE is executing a multi-pronged procurement strategy to secure the least-cost, least-risk resources for customers while capturing federal tax credits that directly support affordability. This strategy includes the 2023 All-Source Request for Proposals (RFP), power purchase agreement (PPA) procurement efforts, and the 2025 RFP — together representing the largest clean energy acquisition effort in company history. These processes are overseen by the Oregon Public Utility Commission (OPUC), which ensures that all bids are evaluated through a fair, impartial, and transparent review process. “Every step in this process is about delivering the most value for our customers,” said John McFarland, Chief Commercial, Customer and Digital Solutions Officer. “By capturing federal tax credits and building the right mix of company-owned and partner projects, we’re adding the energy Oregon needs in a way that supports reliability and keeps long-term costs as low as possible.” More than 1,000 MW of new clean energy and battery storage With contract negotiations complete, PGE and third-party developers will begin construction planning for new clean energy and battery storage projects totaling 1015 MW (42% utility-owned and 58% Power Purchase Agreements). These resources are expected to begin serving customers in 2027 and 2028. Two projects are advancing into development, using existing transmission and interconnection to reduce costs: Biglow Optimization — Sherman County, Ore. 125 MW solar and 125 MW battery storage Target operation: late 2027 PGE-owned; approx. $540 million investment Wheatridge Expansion — Morrow County, Ore. 240 MW solar and 125 MW battery storage Target operation: late 2027 Joint ownership with a third party; PGE owns 110 MW solar and 65 MW storage; approx. $490 million investment PGE also secured power purchase agreements, pending regulatory approval, for two battery storage projects with a total capacity of 400 MW: Meadowlark Battery — Washington County, Ore. 200 MW battery storage Target operation: late 2027, pending OPUC approval Third-party owned; PGE to serve customers through a long-term power purchase agreement. Nottingham Battery — Washington County, Ore. 200 MW battery storage Target operation: 2028, pending OPUC approval Third-party owned; PGE to serve customers through a long-term power purchase agreement. These projects add flexible, fast-responding resources that help balance renewable energy and strengthen reliability during high demand periods and extreme weather. Looking ahead: PGE files Final Shortlist for 2025 RFP To secure the next round of resources to meet customers’ needs, PGE has submitted the Final Shortlist for its 2025 All-Source RFP, which includes 12 non-emitting projects — wind, solar and battery storage with a combination of power purchase agreements and utility ownership. PGE is targeting the end of Q3 2026 to secure agreements for approximately 2,500 MW of additional clean energy and storage. These projects are planned for service in 2028 and 2029.

title: Brunswick Corporation Expands Licensing Strategy Through New Partnership with Changes Inc.
summary: Corporate communications, press releases and news from Brunswick and its family of 60+ marine recreation and technology brands, plus presentations and events.
body_text: Brunswick Corporation Expands Licensing Strategy Through New Partnership with Changes Inc. Download as PDF July 06, 2026 2:00pm EDT Strategic licensing partnership brings Brunswick’s portfolio of iconic marine brands into mainstream lifestyle retail, beginning with a Boston Whaler apparel launch at Abercrombie & Fitch this summer METTAWA, Ill., July 6, 2026 – Brunswick Corporation (NYSE: BC), the global leader in marine recreation, today announced a new licensing partnership with Changes Inc. , a leader in trend-driven licensed apparel, designed to extend Brunswick’s portfolio of brands into mainstream retail and everyday lifestyle fashion. As the first retail activation under the partnership, Boston Whaler , one of Brunswick’s flagship brands, will launch an exclusive limited-edition apparel collection , including graphic tees and sweatshirts, at Abercrombie & Fitch stores online and in store beginning July 2026. A Strategic, Multi-Brand Licensing Platform Brunswick selected Changes Inc. as a licensing partner based on its on-trend design and apparel execution, established relationships with premier lifestyle retailers and their proven ability to translate heritage brands into culturally relevant fashion. The partnership gives Brunswick the credibility and speed to enter lifestyle retail environments at scale. The agreement extends beyond the Boston Whaler and Abercrombie & Fitch program and includes the rights to additional Brunswick brands, including Mercury Marine and Mercury Racing, with future placements expected as the program expands into new retail partners over time. “This partnership with Changes Inc., is about building a long-term, multi-brand platform that extends Brunswick’s reach into non-endemic retail environments that connect with consumers long before they ever step foot on a boat,” said Nicole DaPra, Licensing Manager, Brunswick Corporation. “Boston Whaler’s launch at Abercrombie & Fitch showcases this strategic enterprise initiative, enabling us to engage younger audiences, build brand awareness earlier in the consumer journey and meet consumers where they already are.” First Retail Activation: Boston Whaler x Abercrombie & Fitch The inaugural collection under the partnership features Boston Whaler, translating the brand’s decade of marine heritage into modern, trend-forward graphic tees and sweatshirts. As the program scales, Brunswick expects to announce additional brands, retail partners, and product categories, further increasing the visibility of its portfolio in non-traditional retail spaces. “Brunswick has the strongest portfolio of heritage brands in the recreational marine category, and we see significant opportunity to bring that portfolio into mainstream retail over time,” said Will Thompson, Vice President of Licensing, Changes. “Boston Whaler’s launch at Abercrombie & Fitch is just the start. We are proud to be Brunswick’s partner in building a licensing platform that can scale across brands and retailers in the years ahead.” To view the Boston Whaler x Abercrombie & Fitch collection online, click here . About Brunswick Corporation Brunswick Corporation (NYSE: BC) is a global leader in marine recreation, delivering innovation that transforms experiences on the water and beyond. Its technology-driven solutions are informed by deep consumer insights and guided by the belief that “Next Never Rests™.” Brunswick is home to more than 60 industry-leading brands across marine propulsion (including Mercury Marine), parts and accessories (including Attwood), and marine electronics (including Simrad and Lowrance), as well as boat brands including Boston Whaler, Sea Ray, Bayliner, Lund, and Harris. Headquartered in Mettawa, Illinois, Brunswick has approximately 14,000 employees operating in 26 countries. Learn more at Brunswick.com. About Changes, Inc. Headquartered in New York, Changes is a trusted, “Best In Class”, apparel company known as experts in pop culture. Changes is a global leader in design, manufacturing and distribution. Established in 1977, the company partners with some of the best known entertainment and consumer brands such as Paramount, Jack Daniel’s and Sony Consumer Products. Released July 6, 2026

title: Stronger together - Electric Air and Helios Climate.
body_text: We're excited to announce that Electric Air and Helios Climate Industries have merged. We're bringing together experience from renewables, automotive and aerospace to tackle a hugely important challenge — building electrification. Today Electric Air is a tech enabled HVAC contractor focused on providing the best heating and cooling systems for homeowners while reducing the upfront and operational costs of these systems. Electric Air was founded by Chris Mui, focusing on developing next generation heat pump systems. We continue this effort with our work on sophisticated heat pump controls and improving the homeowner experience both in the purchasing process, as well as normal operation. Electric Air is funded by Y Combinator and participated in the Winter 23 batch. Helios Climate Industries was founded by Jeremy Osborne and Shreyas Sudhakar and went through the Summer 2023 batch of Y Combinator. After talking to homeowners across the US interested in heat pumps they realized that cost of installation was one of the main barriers to adoption; in many cases it wipes out potential energy savings. They set out to build a company focused on driving down the cost of installs through improvements to labor, software and hardware. We're really excited by the capabilities of the combined team, and look forward to electrifying your home heating and cooling!
